newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile copper output seen at 4.8 mln T in 2000.
newsitem.headline: Chile copper output seen at 4.8 mln T in 2000.

text.p: Chilean copper production is expected to rise to 3.4 million tonnes this year and climb to 4.8 million tonnes by 2000 as a result of new mines and expansions at existing pits, said private trade group Sonami.
"We are always adjusting our figures, but we see constant growth until at least 2000," Hernan Hochschild, president of the Sociedad Nacional de Mineria (Sonami), told Reuters in an interview.
"An important margin of growth, however, will depend on the increase in demand," he added.
Chile, the world's top copper producer, mined 3.1 million tonnes of the red metal last year.

Figures from Sonami, which represents most private mining companies in Chile, showed that the giant Escondida pit -- fresh from a recent expansion -- is expected to produce 920,000 tonnes of fine copper this year.
Production at Escondida, owned by Broken Hill Proprietary and RTZ Corp plc, is seen rising to one million tonnes by 2000.
The pit, world's largest copper mine, is second only to Chilean state copper company Codelco in terms of output.

Chilean copper production will also be boosted by the start up in coming years of the huge Collahuasi and Los Pelambres pits which will add over 600,000 tonnes a year to the country's red metal output.

Despite soaring output from Chile, world copper prices are likely to remain stable until the end of the decade with the fast-growing Asian economies soaking up much of the increase in copper supplies, he said.
"We expect prices to be in the $0.90-$1.10 range," he said.
"There may be one or two years in which supply exceeds demand. But as developing countries continue growing, the increase in production will be absorbed."

Within Asia, Chile regards China's huge economy as a key market for future copper exports. Chinese consumers use 500 grams of copper per capita a year, compared with around 10 kilograms in industrialized countries, he said.
"There's tremendous space in the Chinese market where we can sell copper," said Hochschild.
Not only do the Chinese want to buy copper concentrates, but they are keen to guarantee their supplies, by purchasing a stake in a medium-sized copper mine, he said.
Chinese officials have held talks with several Chilean-owned mines with a view to possibly financing an expansion at one of the pits, he said.
